There are a number of "states" in which an individual in this dataset are assigned; 1. Has meaningful employment 1. In the same county as their high school. 2. In the same region as their high school, but not county. 3. In Minnesota, but not in Southwest Minnesota. 2. Is attending post-secondary. 3. Has a MN employment record but it's not meaningful, and not attending post-secondary. 4. Does not have a MN employment record and is not attending post-secondary. There are three "times" in which we checked to see if the individual had meaningful employment within these geographies; 1. one year after graduating high school 2. five years after graduation, and 3. ten years after graduation. Meaningful employment is determined by whether an individual worked 1,000 hours for an employer during time X. In addition, if the individual is working for an employer but not meaningful at time X but worked 1,000 hours for that employer during another year it's still considered "meaningful". Due to time x potentially being passed the date of the latest data (2023) for some individuals, the analysis below will filter out all individuals where time x is after 2023. From the multiple correspondence analysis and the principle component analysis we determined that the following independent variables will be included in the analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} updated.master %>% select(-PersonID, -grad.year.1, -grad.year.5, -grad.year.10) %>% lapply(class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $Gender [1] "character" $economic.status [1] "numeric" $SpecialEdStatus [1] "numeric" $RaceEthnicity [1] "character" $english.learner [1] "numeric" $non.english.home [1] "numeric" $Dem_Desc [1] "factor" $edr [1] "factor" $pseo.participant [1] "factor" $took.ACT [1] "factor" $ap.exam [1] "factor" $cte.achievement [1] "factor" $attended.ps [1] "factor" $ps.grad [1] "factor" $ps.grad.InstitutionSector [1] "factor" $highest.cred.level [1] "factor" $ps.grad.location [1] "factor" $ps.grad.in.same.ruca [1] "factor" $ps.grad.in.same.edr [1] "factor" $ps.grad.in.same.pr [1] "factor" $ps.grad.in.MN [1] "factor" $ACTCompositeScore [1] "numeric" $total.cte.courses.taken [1] "numeric" $MCA.M [1] "numeric" $MCA.R [1] "numeric" $MCA.S [1] "numeric" $avg.unemp.rate [1] "numeric" $avg.wages.pct.state [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: # Methodology For this analysis we are keeping it simple. For categorical variables I’ll be using the Cramer’s v-square measure of association. The V\^2 value is from 0 to 1 with 0 meaning there’s no association and a value closer to 1 indicates a strong association. | **Cramér’s V Value** | **Interpretation** | |----------------------|----------------------------------| | 0.00–0.10 | Negligible association | | 0.10–0.20 | Weak | | 0.20–0.40 | Moderate | | 0.40–0.60 | Relatively strong | | 0.60–0.80 | Strong | | 0.80–1.00 | Very strong (possibly redundant) | For the variables with continuous values I’ll be using the Wilcoxon two paired groups test. P-value will be used to determine whether we can reject the NULL hypothesis at a .01 level. I’ll also include boxplots to see in which direction there might be influence from the variables. We are going to split up the analysis into two different datasets. The first dataset will combine 3 of the previous states into one. - Has meaningful employment anywhere in Southwest Minnesota, which combines the following states; - Meaningful emp County - Meaningful emp region The remaining states will stay the same. - Has meaningful employment in Minnesota, but not in Southwest Minnesota - Is attending a post-secondary institution. - Has a MN employment record but it's not meaningful, and they are not attending post-secondary. - Does not have a MN employment record and is not attending post-secondary. We have quite a few variables remaining, even after MCA analysis. So let's take a look at how we are going to proceed and group all of this together to see how these relationships work. - Demographics - `Gender` - `economic.status` - `SpecialEdStatus` - `RaceEthnicity` - `englisher.learner` - `non.english.home` - High school characteristics - `Dem_Desc` - `edr` - `avg.unemp.rate` - `avg.wage.pct.state` - High school accomplishments - `pseo.participant` - `took.ACT` - `ACTCompositeScore` - `ap.exam` - MCA scores - `MCA.M` - `MCA.R` - `MCA.S` - `cte.achievement` - `total.cte.courses.taken` - Post-secondary - `attended.ps` - `ps.grad` - `ps.grad.InstitutionSector` - `highest.cred.level` - `ps.grad.location`

# Demographics In the demographics section we will examine the relationship between that paths taken by individuals and the following variables; - Demographics - `Gender` - `economic.status` - `SpecialEdStatus` - `RaceEthnicity` - `englisher.learner` - `non.english.home`
## Summary of Demographic Variables and Workforce Participation Outcomes The following demographic variables were examined in relation to workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation using cross-tabulation analysis and Cramer's V. Variables are ranked by the strength of their association at year 1, as this represents the period of greatest differentiation across all variables. **1. Economic Status** (Cramer's V: 0.285, 0.127, 0.094) The strongest demographic predictor of workforce participation outcomes, particularly at year 1. Economically disadvantaged students enter the workforce earlier but into less stable employment, while non-disadvantaged students pursue postsecondary education at much higher rates. Differences narrow considerably by years 5 and 10. **2. Special Education Status** (Cramer's V: 0.265, 0.149, 0.097) The second strongest demographic predictor, with a notably distinct pattern of earlier workforce entry into less stable employment and much lower postsecondary attendance. A consistent tendency toward meaningful regional rather than Minnesota employment persists across all three time points. **3. English Learner Status** (Cramer's V: 0.214, 0.086, 0.059) A moderate association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time. English learners enter the workforce earlier but into less stable situations, with persistent challenges in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment through year 10. **4. Non-English Home Language** (Cramer's V: 0.178, 0.058, 0.047) Closely mirrors the English learner pattern across all three time points, consistent with the strong overlap between these variables identified during MCA. Slightly weaker associations than English learner status at all time points. **5. Race/Ethnicity** (Cramer's V: 0.108, 0.044, 0.047) A weak but statistically significant association that declines sharply after year 1. Notable patterns include lower postsecondary attendance among Hispanic and AI students at year 1, persistent workforce challenges for AI students, and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record among all minority groups at year 10. **6. Gender** (Cramer's V: 0.097, 0.093, 0.056) The weakest demographic predictor overall, with consistently weak associations across all three time points. Females are more likely to pursue postsecondary education immediately after graduation while males transition more quickly into regional employment, though differences narrow considerably by year 10.
## `Gender` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between gender and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. While statistically significant at all three time points, Cramer's V values indicate a weak association throughout. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, the most notable gender difference is in postsecondary attendance, with females attending at a higher rate (60.9%) than males (52.1%). Males show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (14.4% vs 10.9%) and are more likely to have no Minnesota employment record (12.0% vs 8.6%), suggesting males transition more quickly into the workforce while females are more likely to pursue postsecondary education immediately after graduation. (χ²=449.730, df=4, Cramer's V=0.097, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation, gender differences in postsecondary attendance persist but narrow, with females still attending at a higher rate (19.8% vs 14.1%). Males continue to show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (26.2% vs 20.9%), while females show slightly higher rates of no Minnesota employment record (22.6% vs 24.4%). (χ²=303.350, df=4, Cramer's V=0.093, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation, gender differences narrow considerably, with Cramer's V declining to 0.056. Males maintain a modest advantage in meaningful regional employment (26.3% vs 23.2%) and meaningful Minnesota employment (24.7% vs 22.4%), while females show higher rates of no Minnesota employment record (37.8% vs 34.7%), potentially reflecting differences in out-of-state migration or labor force participation patterns. (χ²=61.851, df=3, Cramer's V=0.056, p\<0.001) **Summary** Gender shows a statistically significant but consistently weak association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points. The most notable pattern is that females are more likely to pursue postsecondary education immediately after graduation while males transition more quickly into regional employment, though these differences narrow considerably by year 10.

## `RaceEthnicity` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between race/ethnicity and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. While statistically significant at all three time points, Cramer's V values indicate a weak association overall, with the strength of association declining sharply from year 1 to years 5 and 10. Interpretation of minority group results should be made with caution given the relatively small sample sizes for AI, Asian/PI, Black, and Hispanic students in this Southwest Minnesota dataset. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, race/ethnicity shows a weak but meaningful association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.108). White students show the highest rate of postsecondary attendance (60.7%), compared to considerably lower rates for Hispanic (28.0%), Black (44.4%), and AI students (31.7%). Hispanic (20.1%) and Black (18.4%) students show notably higher rates of meaningful regional employment than White students (11.5%), while AI students show the highest combined rates of not meaningful employment (30.6%) and no Minnesota employment record (26.2%), suggesting significant early workforce challenges for this group. (χ²=1942.573, df=16, Cramer's V=0.108, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens dramatically (Cramer's V=0.044). Hispanic students show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (25.2%), while AI students show the lowest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (7.8%) and the highest combined rates of not meaningful employment (27.3%) and no Minnesota employment record (28.6%). Asian/PI and Black students show relatively higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (18.1% and 19.1% respectively), suggesting these groups may be pursuing employment outside the region at higher rates. (χ²=278.357, df=16, Cramer's V=0.044, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer's V=0.047). A notable pattern emerges with Asian/PI (42.6%), Black (39.1%), Hispanic (40.0%), and AI (37.6%) students all showing higher rates of no Minnesota employment record compared to White students (35.7%), suggesting higher rates of out-of-state migration or labor force non-participation among minority groups in the long term. AI students continue to show the lowest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (10.1%), while Asian/PI and Black students maintain relatively higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (25.0% and 23.0% respectively). (χ²=133.122, df=12, Cramer's V=0.047, p\<0.001) **Summary** Race/ethnicity shows a statistically significant but consistently weak association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points, with the association declining sharply after year 1. The most notable patterns are the lower rates of postsecondary attendance among Hispanic and AI students at year 1, the persistent workforce challenges faced by AI students across all time points, and the higher rates of no Minnesota employment record among all minority groups at year 10 relative to White students. ## `non.english.home` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between non-English home language (0 = English speaking home, 1 = non-English speaking home) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. The pattern of results closely mirrors that of English learner status, which is expected given the strong overlap between these two variables identified during MCA. The association is moderate at year 1 and weakens considerably over time. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, non-English home language shows a moderate association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.178), somewhat weaker than the English learner association at the same time point. Students from English speaking homes are far more likely to be attending postsecondary education (59.1% vs 31.0%), while students from non-English speaking homes show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (19.6% vs 12.0%), not meaningful employment (21.5% vs 15.8%), and no Minnesota employment record (22.1% vs 9.1%), consistent with earlier workforce entry but less stable employment outcomes. (χ²=1519.246, df=4, Cramer's V=0.178, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens dramatically (Cramer's V=0.058). Rates of meaningful regional employment converge almost entirely between the two groups (22.6% vs 23.7%). Students from non-English speaking homes continue to show lower rates of postsecondary attendance (12.8% vs 17.3%) and meaningful Minnesota employment (14.5% vs 18.5%), and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record (29.7% vs 22.9%), patterns nearly identical to those observed for English learners at year 5. (χ²=120.330, df=4, Cramer's V=0.058, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association is very weak (Cramer's V=0.047). The most notable remaining differences are in meaningful Minnesota employment (18.4% vs 23.9%) and no Minnesota employment record (42.5% vs 35.7%), consistent with the patterns observed for English learner status at year 10. Rates of meaningful regional employment remain similar between the two groups (21.5% vs 25.0%). (χ²=45.168, df=3, Cramer's V=0.047, p\<0.001) **Summary** Non-English home language shows a moderate association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer's V=0.178) that weakens considerably over time, reaching very weak levels by year 10 (Cramer's V=0.047). The results closely mirror those observed for English learner status across all three time points, consistent with the strong overlap between these variables identified during MCA. The primary persistent pattern is a lower rate of meaningful Minnesota employment and higher rate of no Minnesota employment record among students from non-English speaking homes, while rates of meaningful regional employment converge substantially by year 5, suggesting that when students from non-English speaking homes do achieve stable employment they are roughly as likely as their peers to find it within the region. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, non.english.home) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$non.english.home, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/Demographics/non-english-home-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

# High school characteristics We will take a look at the following variables; - High school characteristics - `Dem_Desc` - `edr` - `avg.unemp.rate` - `avg.wage.pct.state`
## Summary of High School Characteristics Variables and Workforce Participation Outcomes The following high school characteristics variables were examined in relation to workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Categorical variables were examined using cross-tabulation and Cramer's V, while continuous variables were examined using one-way ANOVA with eta-squared as the measure of effect size. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists reflecting their respective effect size measures. **Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer's V at Year 1** 1. EDR (Cramer's V: 0.079, 0.110, 0.124) The stronger of the two categorical predictors and notable for its increasing association over time. EDR 6E Southwest Central students show a persistent and growing advantage in meaningful Minnesota employment, while EDR 8 Southwest students show increasing rates of no Minnesota employment record over time, suggesting higher out-of-state migration from the more rural southwestern portion of the region. 2. Community Demographic Description (Cramer's V: 0.057, 0.072, 0.079) A weak but consistently strengthening association across all three time points. Urban/town/rural mix students increasingly gravitate toward meaningful Minnesota employment outside the region, while town/rural mix and entirely rural students show stronger and more persistent attachment to regional employment. **Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared at Year 1** 1. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²: 0.010, 0.004, 0.006) Despite being the stronger of the two continuous predictors at year 1, the effect size is negligible across all time points, explaining at most 1% of variance in workforce participation outcomes. A consistent finding is that meaningful regional employment shows higher relative wages than meaningful Minnesota employment across all three time points, suggesting Southwest Minnesota offers competitive wages relative to the broader state labor market. 2. Average Unemployment Rate (η²: 0.005, 0.015, 0.032) The weaker predictor at year 1 but showing a growing association over time, reaching a small effect size by year 10. The most consistent finding is that individuals with no Minnesota employment record experience lower average unemployment rates, likely reflecting out-of-state migration to stronger labor markets. **Overall Pattern** Both categorical and continuous high school characteristics variables show weak to negligible associations with workforce participation outcomes, with effect sizes that are among the smallest observed across all variable groups examined. The most substantively meaningful finding is the persistent geographic sorting pattern across both EDR and community type — students from more urban and centrally located communities show increasing tendencies toward employment outside the region, while students from more rural and peripheral communities show stronger regional workforce attachment. This geographic sorting strengthens over time and represents the most actionable finding from the high school characteristics group for regional workforce development planning.
## `Dem_Desc` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between community demographic description (Town/rural mix, Urban/town/rural mix, Entirely rural) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Community type shows a weak but statistically significant association across all three time points, with the association actually strengthening slightly from year 1 to years 5 and 10, an unusual pattern relative to the demographic variables examined previously. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, community type shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.057). The most notable difference is that entirely rural students show a higher rate of postsecondary attendance (64.3%) compared to town/rural mix (55.1%) and urban/town/rural mix (55.5%) students. Town/rural mix students show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (13.8%), while urban/town/rural mix students show the highest rate of not meaningful employment (18.4%). (χ²=309.223, df=8, Cramer's V=0.057, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association strengthens modestly (Cramer's V=0.072). Urban/town/rural mix students show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (25.4% vs 17.3% and 15.4%), suggesting students from more urban communities are more likely to find employment outside the region. Town/rural mix students show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (25.0%), while entirely rural students show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (27.4%). (χ²=363.860, df=8, Cramer's V=0.072, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak but statistically significant (Cramer's V=0.079). The most striking pattern is that urban/town/rural mix students show a much higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (33.2% vs 22.0% and 20.9%) but a notably lower rate of meaningful regional employment (16.5% vs 26.4% and 25.7%), confirming that students from more urban communities are considerably more likely to find employment outside the region in the long term. Entirely rural students show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (38.6%). (χ²=250.931, df=6, Cramer's V=0.079, p\<0.001) **Summary** Community type shows a weak but statistically significant and remarkably consistent association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points, with the strength of association slightly increasing over time — the opposite pattern from most demographic variables. The most substantively important finding is the persistent and growing divergence between urban/town/ rural mix students, who increasingly gravitate toward meaningful Minnesota employment outside the region, and town/rural mix and entirely rural students, who show stronger attachment to regional employment. This geographic sorting pattern becomes more pronounced at years 5 and 10, suggesting community of origin has a lasting influence on where individuals ultimately settle for employment. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, Dem_Desc) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$Dem_Desc, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/High school characteristics/Dem_Desc-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

## `edr` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between Economic Development Region (EDR 6E Southwest Central, EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley, EDR 8 Southwest) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. EDR shows a weak association at year 1 that strengthens notably over time, mirroring the pattern observed for community demographic description and suggesting that geographic origin has an increasing influence on long-term workforce participation outcomes. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, EDR shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.079). EDR 8 Southwest students show the highest rate of postsecondary attendance (60.2%) while EDR 6E Southwest Central students show the lowest (51.6%). EDR 6E students show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment (14.2%) and not meaningful employment (19.4%), while EDR 8 Southwest students show the lowest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (2.9%) compared to EDR 6E (5.8%) and EDR 6W (3.9%). (χ²=600.491, df=8, Cramer's V=0.079, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association strengthens considerably (Cramer's V=0.110). The most striking pattern is the divergence in meaningful Minnesota employment, with EDR 6E Southwest Central students showing a much higher rate (25.0%) compared to EDR 6W (15.5%) and EDR 8 Southwest (13.9%). EDR 8 Southwest students show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (27.4%), while EDR 6E shows the lowest (17.9%), suggesting that students from the Southwest Central region are considerably more likely to remain employed in Minnesota. (χ²=858.413, df=8, Cramer's V=0.110, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association strengthens further (Cramer's V=0.124). EDR 6E Southwest Central students show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (32.4% vs 21.1% and 17.4%), while EDR 8 Southwest students show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (42.1% vs 35.7% and 29.3%). Rates of meaningful regional employment are relatively similar across all three EDRs (22.2%, 26.7%, and 26.0%), suggesting that when students from any region do achieve meaningful regional employment they do so at comparable rates, but EDR 6E students are considerably more likely to find stable employment elsewhere in Minnesota rather than leaving the state entirely. (χ²=612.569, df=6, Cramer's V=0.124, p\<0.001) **Summary** EDR shows a weak but growing association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points, with Cramer's V increasing from 0.079 at year 1 to 0.124 at year 10. The most substantively important finding is the persistent and growing advantage of EDR 6E Southwest Central students in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment, likely reflecting the influence of Marshall and other larger urban centers in that region providing broader employment opportunities. EDR 8 Southwest students show a consistent and growing tendency toward no Minnesota employment record over time, suggesting higher rates of out-of-state migration from the more rural southwestern portion of the region. ## `avg.unemp.rate` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in average unemployment rate experienced by individuals across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. While statistically significant at all three time points, eta-squared values indicate a small and growing association, suggesting that average unemployment rate explains a modest but increasing proportion of variance in workforce participation outcomes over time. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, average unemployment rate differs significantly across outcome groups (F=58.91, df=4, p\<0.001), however the effect size is small (η²=0.005), indicating that unemployment rate explains less than 1% of the variance in workforce participation outcomes at this time point. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests reveal that individuals in the not meaningful employment group experienced significantly higher average unemployment rates than all other groups, while no significant difference was found between the attending postsecondary and no Minnesota employment record groups. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association grows modestly (F=128.82, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.015), remaining a small effect. The meaningful Minnesota employment group is now clearly distinguished from all other groups, experiencing significantly higher average unemployment rates than the meaningful regional employment group. The no Minnesota employment record group experiences significantly lower average unemployment rates than all other groups except meaningful regional employment, suggesting individuals with no Minnesota employment record may have relocated to areas with lower unemployment. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association reaches its strongest point (F=217.93, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.032), though still representing a small effect by conventional benchmarks. The no Minnesota employment record group continues to experience significantly lower average unemployment rates than all other groups, while the meaningful Minnesota employment group experiences significantly higher unemployment rates than the meaningful regional employment group, suggesting that individuals remaining in Minnesota but outside the region face a more challenging labor market environment over time. **Summary** Average unemployment rate shows a statistically significant but small association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (η²=0.005, 0.015, 0.032), with the effect size growing over time. The most consistent finding is that individuals with no Minnesota employment record experience lower average unemployment rates, likely reflecting out-of-state migration to areas with stronger labor markets. ## `avg.wages.pct.state` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in average wages as a percentage of the state average across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. While statistically significant at all three time points, eta-squared values indicate a very small association throughout, suggesting that average wages as a percentage of state average explains only a negligible proportion of variance in workforce participation outcomes. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, average wages as a percentage of state average differs significantly across outcome groups (F=115.79, df=4, p\<0.001), however the effect size is very small (η²=0.010), indicating that this variable explains approximately 1% of the variance in workforce participation outcomes. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests reveal that the attending postsecondary group shows the highest relative wages, significantly higher than both meaningful regional employment and meaningful Minnesota employment groups. The meaningful regional employment group shows significantly higher relative wages than both the meaningful Minnesota employment and not meaningful employment groups, suggesting that regional employment offers competitive wages relative to other employment outcomes at this early stage. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens further (F=38.20, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.004), explaining less than half a percent of variance in workforce participation outcomes. The meaningful regional employment group continues to show significantly higher relative wages than the meaningful Minnesota employment group, while no significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and either the attending postsecondary or no Minnesota employment record groups, suggesting wages in the region are converging with state averages for those in stable employment by year 5. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains very small (F=41.17, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.006). The meaningful regional employment group continues to show significantly higher relative wages than the meaningful Minnesota employment group and not meaningful employment group. No significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and the no Minnesota employment record group, consistent with the pattern observed at year 5. **Summary** Average wages as a percentage of state average shows a statistically significant but negligible association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (η²=0.010, 0.004, 0.006). Despite the very small effect sizes, a consistent and substantively interesting finding is that the meaningful regional employment group shows significantly higher relative wages than the meaningful Minnesota employment group across all three time points, suggesting that regional employment in Southwest Minnesota offers competitive wages relative to employment elsewhere in the state. # High School Accomplishments We are going to analyze the following variables; - High school accomplishments - `pseo.participant` - `took.ACT` - `ACTCompositeScore` - `ap.exam` - MCA scores - `MCA.M` - `MCA.R` - `MCA.S` - `cte.achievement` - `total.cte.courses.taken`
## Summary of High School Accomplishment Variables and Workforce Participation Outcomes The following high school accomplishment variables were examined in relation to workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Categorical variables were examined using cross-tabulation and Cramer's V, while continuous variables were examined using one-way ANOVA with eta-squared as the measure of effect size. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists reflecting their respective effect size measures. **Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer's V at Year 1** 1. ACT Participation (Cramer's V: 0.430, 0.225, 0.137) The strongest categorical predictor at year 1 and the strongest overall association observed across all variable groups examined. Students who did not take the ACT transition directly into the workforce at much higher rates and show stronger and persistent attachment to regional employment across all time points, while ACT takers are strongly associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent out-of-region employment. 2. PSEO Participation (Cramer's V: 0.370, 0.165, 0.087) The second strongest categorical predictor at year 1, largely reflecting the direct relationship between PSEO participation and continued postsecondary attendance. PSEO participants show a persistent tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment over regional employment at years 5 and 10, suggesting PSEO participation is associated with broader geographic mobility in long-term workforce outcomes. 3. AP Exam Participation (Cramer's V: 0.217, 0.146, 0.089) A moderate association at year 1 that weakens over time, closely mirroring the ACT participation pattern. AP exam participants show the highest postsecondary attendance rate of any subgroup examined (81.4% at year 1) and a persistent tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment over regional employment at years 5 and 10. 4. CTE Achievement (Cramer's V: 0.075, 0.090, 0.088) The weakest categorical predictor at year 1 but with a remarkably stable and substantively important pattern across all three time points. CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment at every time point, with a clear dose-response relationship across CTE engagement levels. No CTE students show strikingly high rates of no Minnesota employment record by year 10 (43.8%), suggesting CTE participation is strongly associated with long-term regional retention. **Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared at Year 1** 1. MCA Math (η²: 0.168, 0.025, 0.017) The strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, the largest observed for any continuous variable examined. A distinctive early pattern shows both not meaningful employment and no Minnesota employment record groups scoring significantly lower than meaningful regional employment — unique among MCA subjects at year 1. By year 10 the meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest Math scores of all groups, indistinguishable from not meaningful employment. 2. MCA Reading (η²: 0.129, 0.023, 0.057) The second strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, notable for its unique trajectory — weakening to a small effect at year 5 before strengthening to a medium effect at year 10, the only continuous variable to show this pattern. By year 10 the meaningful regional employment group is indistinguishable from not meaningful employment in Reading scores, with both groups significantly below meaningful Minnesota employment and no Minnesota employment record. 3. MCA Science (η²: 0.085, 0.033, 0.019) A large effect at year 1 that weakens to a small effect over time. The voluntary nature of Science MCA participation creates a self-selected sample of higher-achieving students, which should be considered when interpreting results. The pattern mirrors Reading and Math, with the meaningful regional employment group consistently showing the lowest Science scores and being indistinguishable from not meaningful employment across all time points. 4. ACT Composite Score (η²: 0.093, 0.038, 0.028) A moderate effect at year 1 that weakens to a small effect over time. The attending postsecondary group shows substantially higher ACT scores than all workforce-engaged groups throughout, and the meaningful regional employment group shows progressively lower ACT scores relative to other groups, with the no Minnesota employment record group consistently showing higher scores than not meaningful employment at years 5 and 10. 5. Total CTE Courses Taken (η²: 0.032, 0.027, 0.028) A small but remarkably stable effect across all three time points, unique among continuous variables in showing no meaningful decline over time. The meaningful regional employment group shows the highest number of CTE courses taken at every time point, with the gap between regional and out-of-region employment groups growing from no significant difference at year 1 to approximately 1.3 courses by year 10. 6. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²: 0.010, 0.004, 0.006) A negligible effect across all three time points, explaining at most 1% of variance in workforce participation outcomes. Despite the very small effect size, a consistent finding is that meaningful regional employment shows higher relative wages than meaningful Minnesota employment across all time points, suggesting Southwest Minnesota offers competitive wages relative to the broader state labor market. 7. Average Unemployment Rate (η²: 0.005, 0.015, 0.032) The weakest predictor at year 1 but showing a growing association over time, reaching a small effect size by year 10. The most consistent finding is that individuals with no Minnesota employment record experience lower average unemployment rates, likely reflecting out-of-state migration to stronger labor markets. **Overall Pattern** A clear and consistent theme emerges across the high school accomplishment variables that has direct implications for regional workforce development. Academic achievement indicators — ACT participation, AP exam, PSEO, and all three MCA subjects — are associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent employment outside the region, with higher achievers increasingly gravitating toward meaningful Minnesota employment or out-of-state migration over time. CTE engagement indicators tell the opposite story — both CTE achievement level and total CTE courses taken are consistently associated with stronger and more persistent regional workforce attachment across all three time points. This divergence between academic and CTE pathways is one of the most substantively important findings of the entire analysis, suggesting that CTE programming plays a meaningful role in regional workforce retention in Southwest Minnesota even if the statistical effect sizes are modest.
## `pseo.participant` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between PSEO participation (0 = did not participate, 1 = participated) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Analysis is restricted to individuals with known PSEO participation status, excluding the 2008-2010 graduation cohorts where PSEO data was unavailable. PSEO participation shows the strongest association of any high school accomplishment variable at year 1, with the association weakening considerably over time. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, PSEO participation shows a moderate to strong association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.370), the strongest association observed for any variable examined thus far. PSEO participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary education (77.7% vs 40.8%), while non-participants show substantially higher rates of meaningful regional employment (17.1% vs 7.5%), not meaningful employment (21.6% vs 8.4%), and no Minnesota employment record (15.0% vs 3.6%). This pattern strongly reflects the design of PSEO — participants are by definition already engaged in postsecondary education while still in high school and are therefore much more likely to continue into postsecondary after graduation. (χ²=5121.797, df=4, Cramer's V=0.370, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens substantially (Cramer's V=0.165). PSEO participants now show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (21.6% vs 16.5%) and postsecondary attendance (21.8% vs 11.8%), while non-participants show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (26.1% vs 20.2%) and no Minnesota employment record (26.0% vs 21.7%). The reversal in meaningful regional versus Minnesota employment rates between the two groups is notable, suggesting PSEO participants are more likely to find employment outside the region by year 5. (χ²=680.833, df=4, Cramer's V=0.165, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens considerably (Cramer's V=0.087). PSEO participants show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (27.8% vs 20.6%), while non-participants show a higher rate of meaningful regional employment (25.0% vs 21.2%). Rates of no Minnesota employment record converge almost entirely between the two groups (37.4% vs 38.0%), suggesting that long-term out-of-state migration patterns are similar regardless of PSEO participation. (χ²=74.460, df=3, Cramer's V=0.087, p\<0.001) **Summary** PSEO participation shows the strongest association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 of any variable examined (Cramer's V=0.370), largely reflecting the direct relationship between PSEO participation and continued postsecondary attendance. As this immediate effect dissipates, the association weakens considerably by years 5 and 10. A consistent and substantively important pattern emerges over time — PSEO participants are more likely to find meaningful employment outside the region while non-participants show stronger attachment to regional employment, suggesting that PSEO participation may be associated with broader geographic mobility in long-term workforce participation. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, pseo.participant) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023", pseo.participant != is.na(pseo.participant)) %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$pseo.participant, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/High school accomplishments/pseo-participant-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

## `ACTCompositeScore` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in ACT composite score across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation, restricted to individuals who took the ACT. While statistically significant at all three time points, eta-squared values indicate a moderate effect at year 1 that weakens over time, suggesting that ACT composite score explains a meaningful proportion of variance in workforce participation outcomes particularly in the early post-graduation period. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, ACT composite score differs significantly across outcome groups (F=799.65, df=4, p\<0.001) with a moderate effect size (η²=0.093). The attending postsecondary group shows substantially higher ACT scores than all other groups (estimate=3.50 vs meaningful regional employment, p\<0.001), reflecting the strong relationship between academic achievement and postsecondary attendance. The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than the meaningful regional employment group (estimate=0.84, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between the meaningful regional employment, not meaningful employment, and no Minnesota employment record groups, suggesting ACT score does not meaningfully distinguish between these three non-postsecondary outcomes at year 1. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens but remains a small to moderate effect (F=225.44, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.038). The attending postsecondary group continues to show the highest ACT scores, significantly higher than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment group now shows significantly higher scores than the meaningful regional employment group (estimate=1.84, p\<0.001). Notably, the no Minnesota employment record group shows significantly higher scores than the not meaningful employment group (estimate=0.94, p\<0.001), suggesting that individuals who leave Minnesota without a record tend to have higher academic achievement than those who remain with unstable employment. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens further to a small effect (F=114.55, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.028). The meaningful regional employment group now shows the lowest ACT scores of all groups, significantly lower than meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=1.60, p\<0.001), not meaningful employment (estimate=1.02, p\<0.001), and no Minnesota employment record (estimate=1.71, p\<0.001). The no Minnesota employment record group shows significantly higher scores than the not meaningful employment group (estimate=0.68, p\<0.001), consistent with the pattern observed at year 5. **Summary** ACT composite score shows a moderate association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (η²=0.093) that weakens to a small effect by years 5 and 10 (η²=0.038, 0.028). The most consistent and substantively important finding is that the attending postsecondary group shows substantially higher ACT scores than all workforce-engaged groups, and that the meaningful regional employment group shows progressively lower ACT scores relative to other groups over time. By year 10 the meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest ACT scores of any group, suggesting that higher academic achievement is associated with employment outside the region in the long term. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, ACTCompositeScore) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% drop_na() %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% mutate(q1 = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, .25), q3 = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, .75), iqr = IQR(ACTCompositeScore), low.outlier = q1 - 1.5*iqr, high.outlier = q3 + 1.5*iqr) %>% filter(ACTCompositeScore > low.outlier, ACTCompositeScore < high.outlier) %>% ungroup() labels <- data %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% summarize(Min = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, .0), Q1 = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, .25), Median = median(ACTCompositeScore), Q3 = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, .75), Max = quantile(ACTCompositeScore, 1), Mean = mean(ACTCompositeScore)) %>% ungroup() plot <- ggplot(data, aes(grad.year.1, ACTCompositeScore, fill = grad.year.1, group = grad.year.1)) + geom_boxplot_interactive() + geom_label(data = labels, aes(x = grad.year.1, y = 40, label = paste("Min: ", comma(Min, accuracy = .1), "\nQ1: ", comma(Q1, accuracy = .1), "\nMedian: ", comma(Median, accuracy = .1), "\nQ3: ", comma(Q3, accuracy = .1), "\nMax: ", comma(Max, accuracy = ), "\nMean: ", comma(Mean, accuracy = .1))), color = "white") + labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Boxplots of ACT composite score by employment state")+ scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma, limits = c(0, 45))+ scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu")) + theme_bar+ theme(legend.position = "none", text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = .9)) girafe(ggobj = plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>% girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"), opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

## `ap.exam` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between AP exam participation (0 = did not take AP exam, 1 = took AP exam) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. AP exam participation shows a moderate association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with a pattern broadly similar to ACT participation but somewhat weaker throughout. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, AP exam participation shows a moderate association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.217). AP exam participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary education (81.4% vs 51.9%), the highest postsecondary attendance rate observed for any subgroup across all variables examined. Non-AP exam students show substantially higher rates of meaningful regional employment (14.1% vs 5.2%), not meaningful employment (17.9% vs 7.8%), and no Minnesota employment record (11.6% vs 3.5%), reflecting the strong relationship between AP exam participation and postsecondary education intentions. (χ²=2239.394, df=4, Cramer's V=0.217, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens considerably (Cramer's V=0.146). AP exam participants show notably higher rates of postsecondary attendance (26.7% vs 15.1%) and meaningful Minnesota employment (23.2% vs 17.3%), while non-AP exam students show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (25.3% vs 14.3%). The divergence in meaningful regional versus Minnesota employment between the two groups is pronounced, mirroring the pattern observed for ACT participation and suggesting AP exam participants are more likely to find employment outside the region. (χ²=751.737, df=4, Cramer's V=0.146, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens further (Cramer's V=0.089). AP exam participants continue to show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (30.3% vs 22.2%), while non-AP exam students maintain a higher rate of meaningful regional employment (26.0% vs 18.3%). Rates of no Minnesota employment record are similar between the two groups (38.4% vs 35.8%), suggesting long-term out-of-state migration patterns converge regardless of AP exam participation. (χ²=159.083, df=3, Cramer's V=0.089, p\<0.001) **Summary** AP exam participation shows a moderate association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer's V=0.217) that weakens considerably over time, reaching weak levels by year 10 (Cramer's V=0.089). The pattern closely mirrors that of ACT participation, with AP exam participants showing stronger attachment to postsecondary education at year 1 and a persistent tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment over the regional labor market at years 5 and 10. ## `MCA.R` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in MCA Reading scores across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Note that 2,698 individuals (5.3%) are missing MCA Reading scores and are excluded from this analysis. eta-squared values indicate a large effect at year 1 that weakens considerably by year 5 before strengthening again at year 10, suggesting a complex and evolving relationship between Reading achievement and workforce participation outcomes over time. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, MCA Reading score differs significantly across outcome groups (F=1633.60, df=4, p\<0.001) with a large effect size (η²=0.129). The attending postsecondary group shows the highest Reading scores, significantly higher than all other groups (estimate=0.625 vs meaningful regional employment, p\<0.001). The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.361, p\<0.001). The no Minnesota employment record group shows significantly lower scores than all other groups except not meaningful employment, while no significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens considerably to a small effect (F=180.08, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.023). The attending postsecondary group continues to show the highest Reading scores, significantly higher than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.221, p\<0.001), while the no Minnesota employment record group now shows significantly higher scores than both meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.163, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=0.111, p\<0.001), suggesting that individuals who leave Minnesota tend to have higher Reading achievement than those remaining in unstable regional employment. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association strengthens notably (F=362.29, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.057), reaching a medium effect size — the only ANOVA variable to strengthen to this degree at year 10. The meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest Reading scores of all groups, significantly lower than meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=0.431, p\<0.001) and no Minnesota employment record (estimate=0.418, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between the meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups, nor between meaningful Minnesota employment and no Minnesota employment record groups, suggesting that by year 10 Reading achievement primarily distinguishes regional employment from all other outcomes rather than differentiating among non-regional outcomes. **Summary** MCA Reading score shows a large association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (η²=0.129) that weakens to a small effect at year 5 (η²=0.023) before strengthening to a medium effect at year 10 (η²=0.057) — a unique trajectory among all variables examined. The most substantively important finding is that the meaningful regional employment group shows progressively lower Reading scores relative to other groups over time, becoming indistinguishable from the not meaningful employment group by year 10. This suggests that Reading achievement is strongly associated with long-term employment outside the region, and that regional employment increasingly attracts individuals with lower Reading achievement profiles as careers develop. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, MCA.R) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% drop_na() %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% mutate(q1 = quantile(MCA.R, .25), q3 = quantile(MCA.R, .75), iqr = IQR(MCA.R), low.outlier = q1 - 1.5*iqr, high.outlier = q3 + 1.5*iqr) %>% filter(MCA.R > low.outlier, MCA.R < high.outlier) %>% ungroup() labels <- data %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% summarize(Min = quantile(MCA.R, .0), Q1 = quantile(MCA.R, .25), Median = median(MCA.R), Q3 = quantile(MCA.R, .75), Max = quantile(MCA.R, 1), Mean = mean(MCA.R)) %>% ungroup() plot <- ggplot(data, aes(grad.year.1, MCA.R, fill = grad.year.1, group = grad.year.1)) + geom_boxplot_interactive() + geom_label(data = labels, aes(x = grad.year.1, y = 5, label = paste("Min: ", comma(Min, accuracy = .1), "\nQ1: ", comma(Q1, accuracy = .1), "\nMedian: ", comma(Median, accuracy = .1), "\nQ3: ", comma(Q3, accuracy = .1), "\nMax: ", comma(Max, accuracy = ), "\nMean: ", comma(Mean, accuracy = .1))), color = "white") + labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Boxplots of MCA-Reading score by employment state")+ scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma, limits = c(0, 6))+ scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu")) + theme_bar+ theme(legend.position = "none", text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = .9)) girafe(ggobj = plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>% girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"), opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

## `MCA.S` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in MCA Science scores across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. MCA Science is a voluntary assessment and 9,286 individuals (18.3%) are missing scores, reflecting a combination of data availability limitations and voluntary participation. As discussed in the methodology, individuals who chose to take the Science MCA represent a self-selected group that tends to score higher on Reading and Math assessments, and this self-selection should be considered when interpreting these results. Eta-squared values indicate a large effect at year 1 that weakens considerably over time. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, MCA Science score differs significantly across outcome groups (F=893.11, df=4, p\<0.001) with a large effect size (η²=0.085). The attending postsecondary group shows the highest Science scores, significantly higher than all other groups (estimate=0.519 vs meaningful regional employment, p\<0.001). The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than the meaningful regional employment group (estimate=0.156, p\<0.001). Notably, no significant difference is found between the meaningful regional employment, not meaningful employment, and no Minnesota employment record groups, suggesting that Science achievement does not meaningfully distinguish between these three non-postsecondary outcomes at year 1. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens to a small effect (F=231.81, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.033). The attending postsecondary group continues to show the highest Science scores, significantly higher than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than both meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.290, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=-0.285, p\<0.001). The no Minnesota employment record group now shows significantly higher scores than both meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.176, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=0.172, p\<0.001), suggesting that higher Science achievement is associated with both out-of-region Minnesota employment and out-of-state migration. No significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens further to a small effect (F=81.06, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.019). The meaningful regional employment group continues to show the lowest Science scores, significantly lower than meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=0.250, p\<0.001) and no Minnesota employment record (estimate=0.227, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups, nor between meaningful Minnesota employment and no Minnesota employment record groups, mirroring the pattern observed for MCA Reading at year 10. **Summary** MCA Science score shows a large association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (η²=0.085) that weakens to a small effect by years 5 and 10 (η²=0.033, 0.019). The pattern closely parallels MCA Reading and Math, with the meaningful regional employment group consistently showing the lowest Science scores and being indistinguishable from not meaningful employment across all time points. The absence of significant differences between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups across all three time points is a notable finding, suggesting that Science achievement primarily distinguishes regional employment from out-of-region outcomes rather than from unstable employment. ## `MCA.M` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in MCA Math scores across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Note that 2,349 individuals (4.6%) are missing MCA Math scores and are excluded from this analysis. Eta-squared values indicate a large effect at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with MCA Math showing the strongest effect size of the three MCA subjects at year 1. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, MCA Math score differs significantly across outcome groups (F=2171.45, df=4, p\<0.001) with a large effect size (η²=0.168), the largest observed for any continuous variable examined. The attending postsecondary group shows the highest Math scores, significantly higher than all other groups (estimate=0.722 vs meaningful regional employment, p\<0.001) — the largest single group difference observed across all MCA subjects. The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.137, p\<0.001). Distinctively, both the not meaningful employment (estimate=-0.111, p\<0.001) and no Minnesota employment record (estimate=-0.164, p\<0.001) groups show significantly lower scores than meaningful regional employment — a pattern unique among the three MCA subjects at year 1 — suggesting that Math achievement is associated with stable employment of any kind in the early post-graduation period. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens considerably to a small effect (F=211.84, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.025). The attending postsecondary group continues to show the highest Math scores, significantly higher than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment group shows significantly higher scores than both meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.314, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=-0.352, p\<0.001). The no Minnesota employment record group shows significantly higher scores than both meaningful regional employment (estimate=0.144, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=0.181, p\<0.001), but significantly lower scores than meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=-0.170, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups. **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains a small effect (F=111.29, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.017). The meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest Math scores, significantly lower than meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=0.317, p\<0.001) and no Minnesota employment record (estimate=0.272, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between meaningful regional employment and not meaningful employment groups, nor between meaningful Minnesota employment and no Minnesota employment record groups, consistent with the patterns observed for MCA Reading and Science at year 10. **Summary** MCA Math score shows the largest effect size of the three MCA subjects at year 1 (η²=0.168) — a large effect by conventional benchmarks — that weakens to a small effect by years 5 and 10 (η²=0.025, 0.017). A distinctive pattern at year 1 unique among MCA subjects is that both the not meaningful employment and no Minnesota employment record groups score significantly lower than meaningful regional employment, suggesting that Math achievement is uniquely associated with stable employment of any kind in the early post-graduation period. By years 5 and 10 the pattern converges with Reading and Science, with the meaningful regional employment group showing the lowest Math scores and being indistinguishable from not meaningful employment. This consistent long-term pattern across all three MCA subjects strongly suggests that higher academic achievement is associated with employment outside the region, while regional employment increasingly attracts individuals with lower academic achievement profiles over time. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, MCA.M) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% drop_na() %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% mutate(q1 = quantile(MCA.M, .25), q3 = quantile(MCA.M, .75), iqr = IQR(MCA.M), low.outlier = q1 - 1.5*iqr, high.outlier = q3 + 1.5*iqr) %>% filter(MCA.M > low.outlier, MCA.M < high.outlier) %>% ungroup() labels <- data %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% summarize(Min = quantile(MCA.M, .0), Q1 = quantile(MCA.M, .25), Median = median(MCA.M), Q3 = quantile(MCA.M, .75), Max = quantile(MCA.M, 1), Mean = mean(MCA.M)) %>% ungroup() plot <- ggplot(data, aes(grad.year.1, MCA.M, fill = grad.year.1, group = grad.year.1)) + geom_boxplot_interactive() + geom_label(data = labels, aes(x = grad.year.1, y = 5, label = paste("Min: ", comma(Min, accuracy = .1), "\nQ1: ", comma(Q1, accuracy = .1), "\nMedian: ", comma(Median, accuracy = .1), "\nQ3: ", comma(Q3, accuracy = .1), "\nMax: ", comma(Max, accuracy = ), "\nMean: ", comma(Mean, accuracy = .1))), color = "white") + labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Boxplots of MCA-Math score by employment state")+ scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma, limits = c(0, 6))+ scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu")) + theme_bar+ theme(legend.position = "none", text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = .9)) girafe(ggobj = plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>% girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"), opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

## `cte.achievement` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between CTE achievement (CTE Concentrator or Completor, CTE Participant, No CTE) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. CTE achievement shows a weak but statistically significant and strengthening association across all three time points, with a distinctly different pattern from the academic achievement variables examined previously. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, CTE achievement shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.075). CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (15.1%), compared to CTE Participants (11.4%) and No CTE students (8.7%). Postsecondary attendance rates are relatively similar across all three groups (54.0%, 59.2%, and 58.8% respectively), with No CTE students showing a notably higher rate of no Minnesota employment record (14.0% vs 9.6% and 8.8%). The ordering of groups by meaningful regional employment — with CTE engagement positively associated with regional workforce participation — is a substantively important early signal. (χ²=540.647, df=8, Cramer's V=0.075, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association strengthens modestly (Cramer's V=0.090). The divergence in meaningful regional employment across CTE groups becomes more pronounced, with CTE Concentrators or Completors showing the highest rate (28.2%), followed by CTE Participants (22.4%) and No CTE students (16.2%). Conversely, No CTE students show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (28.7% vs 21.7% and 22.2%) and the highest rate of postsecondary attendance (19.8%), suggesting that students without CTE engagement are both more likely to remain in postsecondary education longer and more likely to leave Minnesota entirely. (χ²=575.702, df=8, Cramer's V=0.090, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak but statistically significant (Cramer's V=0.088). The pattern observed at year 5 strengthens further, with CTE Concentrators or Completors showing the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (29.1%), followed by CTE Participants (23.5%) and No CTE students (16.6%). Rates of meaningful Minnesota employment converge across all three groups (22.7%, 24.4%, and 24.3% respectively), while No CTE students show a strikingly high rate of no Minnesota employment record (43.8% vs 32.7% and 36.5%), suggesting substantially higher long-term out-of-state migration among students without CTE engagement. (χ²=310.756, df=6, Cramer's V=0.088, p\<0.001) **Summary** CTE achievement shows a weak but statistically significant and consistent association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points. Unlike the academic achievement variables examined previously, CTE achievement shows a pattern that is distinctly favorable for regional workforce participation — CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment at every time point, and this advantage grows over time. The clear ordering of groups by meaningful regional employment (Concentrator/Completor \> Participant \> No CTE) across all three years suggests a dose-response relationship between CTE engagement and regional workforce attachment. Conversely, students with no CTE engagement show substantially higher rates of no Minnesota employment record by year 10, suggesting that CTE participation is associated with stronger long-term retention in the regional labor market. This finding stands in notable contrast to the academic achievement variables, where higher achievement was consistently associated with employment outside the region. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, cte.achievement) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$cte.achievement, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/High school accomplishments/cte-achievement-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

## `total.cte.courses.taken` **Overview** One-way ANOVA examined differences in total CTE courses taken across workforce participation outcome groups at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Eta-squared values indicate a small but consistent association across all three time points, with the meaningful regional employment group consistently showing the highest number of CTE courses taken of any group. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, total CTE courses taken differs significantly across outcome groups (F=388.03, df=4, p\<0.001) with a small effect size (η²=0.032). The meaningful regional employment group shows significantly more CTE courses taken than all other groups. The attending postsecondary group shows significantly fewer CTE courses than meaningful regional employment (estimate=-1.674, p\<0.001), as does the no Minnesota employment record group (estimate=-1.782, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment group (estimate=-0.901, p\<0.001). No significant difference is found between meaningful regional and meaningful Minnesota employment groups, suggesting that CTE course-taking does not distinguish between these two stable employment outcomes at year 1. **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association remains a small effect (F=240.62, df=4, p\<0.001, η²=0.027). The meaningful regional employment group continues to show significantly more CTE courses taken than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment group now shows significantly fewer CTE courses than meaningful regional employment (estimate=-0.975, p\<0.001), a distinction that was not significant at year 1, suggesting that CTE course-taking increasingly differentiates regional from out-of-region employment over time. The no Minnesota employment record group shows significantly fewer CTE courses than meaningful regional employment (estimate=-1.316, p\<0.001) and not meaningful employment (estimate=-0.513, p\<0.001). **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains a small effect (F=187.13, df=3, p\<0.001, η²=0.028). The meaningful regional employment group continues to show the highest number of CTE courses taken, significantly more than all other groups. The meaningful Minnesota employment and no Minnesota employment record groups are indistinguishable from each other (estimate=-0.012, p=0.998), while both show significantly fewer CTE courses than meaningful regional employment (estimates of -1.302 and -1.314 respectively, p\<0.001). The not meaningful employment group shows significantly fewer CTE courses than meaningful regional employment (estimate=-0.783, p\<0.001) but significantly more than both meaningful Minnesota employment (estimate=0.519, p\<0.001) and no Minnesota employment record (estimate= -0.531, p\<0.001). **Summary** Total CTE courses taken shows a small but consistent association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (η²=0.032, 0.027, 0.028), notable for its stability rather than decline over time. Despite the modest effect size, the meaningful regional employment group shows the highest number of CTE courses taken at every time point, and the gap between regional and out-of-region employment groups grows over time — from no significant difference between regional and Minnesota employment at year 1 to a difference of approximately 1.3 courses by year 10. Together with the CTE achievement findings, these results provide consistent evidence that CTE participation is associated with stronger long-term regional workforce retention, even if the overall explanatory power of this variable is modest. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, total.cte.courses.taken) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% drop_na() %>% group_by(grad.year.1) %>% mutate(q1 = quantile(total.cte.courses.taken, .25), q3 = quantile(total.cte.courses.taken, .75), iqr = IQR(total.cte.courses.taken), low.outlier = q1 - # Post-secondary We will analyze the following variables; - Post-secondary - `attended.ps` - `ps.grad` - `ps.grad.InstitutionSector` - `highest.cred.level` - `ps.grad.location`
## Summary of Postsecondary Variables and Workforce Participation Outcomes The following postsecondary variables were examined in relation to workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. All variables are categorical and were examined using cross-tabulation and Cramer's V. Variables are ranked by Cramer's V at year 1, with the caveat that several variables show inflated associations at year 1 due to structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category. **Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer's V at Year 1** 1. Postsecondary Attendance (Cramer's V: 0.698, 0.295, 0.108) The strongest association at year 1, largely driven by the near-tautological relationship between postsecondary attendance and the attending postsecondary outcome category. As this structural effect dissipates, the association weakens to weak by year 10. The most substantively important long-term finding is that non-attendees show stronger regional employment attachment while attendees show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment and lower rates of no Minnesota employment record. 2. Postsecondary Graduation (Cramer's V: 0.633, 0.330, 0.130) The second strongest association at year 1, also substantially driven by structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category. By year 10 the association weakens to weak, with the most important finding being that postsecondary graduates show considerably higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment while non-graduates show stronger regional attachment and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record. 3. Highest Credential Level (Cramer's V: 0.378, 0.246, 0.111) A strong association at year 1 that weakens to weak by year 10. A clear and persistent inverse relationship emerges between credential level and regional workforce attachment — sub-baccalaureate credential holders show the strongest regional employment rates across all time points, while bachelor and master degree holders show increasing tendencies toward meaningful Minnesota employment and out-of-state migration. Master degree or higher holders show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record at year 10 (43.3%). 4. Postsecondary Graduation Location (Cramer's V: 0.158, 0.191, 0.162) A weak but remarkably stable and substantively compelling association across all three time points. Regional graduates show the strongest and most persistent attachment to meaningful regional employment at every time point, with rates consistently 10-15 percentage points higher than other graduation location groups by years 5 and 10. PS grad outside MN graduates show the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record, reaching 54.8% by year 10 — the highest rate observed for any subgroup across all variables examined. 5. Postsecondary Graduation Institution Sector (Cramer's V: 0.149, 0.161, 0.125) A weak but consistent association across all three time points. Public 2-year institution graduates show the strongest and most persistent regional employment attachment, with meaningful regional employment rates above 35% at both years 5 and 10. Private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the strongest tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment and out-of-state migration. These findings directly reinforce the graduation location results, as regional institutions are predominantly public 2-year institutions. **Overall Pattern** The postsecondary variables collectively tell a coherent and substantively important story for regional workforce development. In the short term, postsecondary attendance and graduation status dominate the picture, largely reflecting structural relationships with the outcome categories. As these structural effects dissipate over time, a clear and consistent pattern emerges — the type, level, and location of postsecondary education shapes not whether individuals are meaningfully employed, but where they are employed. Sub-baccalaureate credentials, public 2-year institutions, and regional postsecondary graduation are all consistently associated with stronger regional workforce attachment, while higher credential levels, 4-year institutions, and out-of-state graduation are associated with employment outside the region or out of state entirely. The finding that graduating from a regional postsecondary institution is among the strongest predictors of long-term regional workforce retention has direct and actionable implications for regional higher education and workforce development policy.

This is largely driven by the structural relationship between the variable and the outcome — virtually all individuals in the attending postsecondary outcome category attended postsecondary (26,953 of 26,954), making this association near-tautological at year 1.
