## `ps.grad` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between postsecondary graduation (No = did not graduate, Y = graduated) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Note that individuals currently attending postsecondary are excluded from this analysis as their graduation status is not yet determined. Postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with a pattern that closely mirrors postsecondary attendance but with important distinctions in the magnitude and direction of effects. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.633). As with postsecondary attendance, this is substantially driven by the structural relationship between graduation status and the attending postsecondary outcome category — postsecondary graduates show an 83.7% rate of still attending postsecondary at year 1, reflecting those who have completed one credential and are pursuing another. Non-graduates show substantially higher rates of meaningful regional employment (19.3% vs 7.4%), not meaningful employment (31.2% vs 4.7%), and no Minnesota employment record (21.3% vs 1.7%), while graduates show markedly lower rates across all non-postsecondary outcomes at this early stage. (χ²=18207.912, df=4, Cramer's V=0.633, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens considerably but remains moderate (Cramer's V=0.330). Non-graduates show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (25.7% vs 22.0%) and notably higher rates of no Minnesota employment record (30.7% vs 17.9%), while postsecondary graduates show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (20.7% vs 15.1%) and postsecondary attendance (26.2% vs 4.5%). The divergence in no Minnesota employment record between the two groups is particularly striking — non-graduates are nearly twice as likely to have no Minnesota employment record as graduates, suggesting postsecondary graduation is strongly associated with remaining employed in Minnesota. (χ²=3791.997, df=4, Cramer's V=0.330, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens to a weak effect (Cramer's V=0.130). Rates of meaningful regional employment converge almost entirely between non-graduates (24.7%) and graduates (24.8%). Postsecondary graduates show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (27.9% vs 17.9%), while non-graduates show a higher rate of no Minnesota employment record (38.6% vs 34.3%) and not meaningful employment (18.7% vs 13.0%). The convergence in meaningful regional employment rates mirrors the pattern observed for postsecondary attendance, suggesting that by year 10 postsecondary graduation has little bearing on whether individuals are employed in the region but continues to distinguish between the quality and location of employment outcomes. (χ²=341.123, df=3, Cramer's V=0.130, p\<0.001) **Summary** Postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer's V=0.633), largely driven by structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category, that weakens to a weak effect by year 10 (Cramer's V=0.130). The most substantively important finding is the persistent and growing advantage of postsecondary graduates in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment across all time points, while non-graduates show stronger attachment to regional employment and considerably higher rates of no Minnesota employment record. ## `ps.grad.InstitutionSector` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between the sector of postsecondary institution from which individuals graduated (1=Public 4-year, 2=Private not-for-profit 4-year, 4=Public 2-year, 11=Private other) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. This analysis is restricted to postsecondary graduates and those currently attending, excluding individuals who never attended or did not graduate. Institution sector shows a weak but consistent association across all three time points, with substantively meaningful differences in the type of employment achieved across sectors. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, institution sector shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.149). The overwhelming majority of individuals across all sectors are still attending postsecondary at year 1, ranging from 70.5% for public 2-year graduates to 94.3% for public 4-year graduates, reflecting the expected pattern that 4-year institution graduates are more likely to be pursuing additional credentials. Among those in the workforce, public 2-year graduates show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (15.3%), more than double the rate of public 4-year graduates (2.6%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduates (0.9%), suggesting that 2-year institution graduates enter regional employment much more quickly. (χ²=2371.287, df=16, Cramer's V=0.149, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer's V=0.161) but the patterns become considerably more interpretable as postsecondary attendance rates decline. Public 2-year graduates show by far the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (35.6%), more than double that of public 4-year graduates (16.2%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduates (8.9%). Conversely, private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (28.5%), followed by public 4-year graduates (20.8%). Private other graduates show notably lower rates of no Minnesota employment record (8.3%) compared to all other sectors, while private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest rate (24.2%), suggesting considerably higher out-of-state migration among graduates of private 4-year institutions. ## `highest.cred.level` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between highest credential level attained (No college, Some college, Less than Associate Degree, Associate Degree, Attending ps, Bachelor Degree, Master Degree or higher) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Highest credential level shows a strong association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with substantively meaningful patterns in how credential level shapes the type and location of employment achieved. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, highest credential level shows a strong association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.378). At this early stage the results are heavily influenced by the structural relationship between credential level and the attending postsecondary outcome category, with postsecondary attendance rates increasing monotonically with credential level — from 0% for no college to 93.0% for master degree or higher. Among those in the workforce, a clear gradient emerges in meaningful regional employment, declining with higher credential levels — from 21.7% for no college to 1.9% for master degree or higher. Conversely, no college individuals show the highest rates of not meaningful employment (39.7%) and no Minnesota employment record (31.6%). (χ²=27300.114, df=24, Cramer's V=0.378, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association weakens to a moderate effect (Cramer's V=0.246) as credential attainment becomes more fully realized. A notable and substantively important pattern emerges — individuals with less than associate degree (35.1%) and associate degree (32.1%) show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment, considerably higher than bachelor degree (16.5%) and master degree or higher (8.1%) holders. The inverse is true for meaningful Minnesota employment, where bachelor degree (23.5%) and master degree or higher (11.8%) holders show lower regional but higher out-of-region employment rates. Master degree or higher individuals show the highest rate of still attending postsecondary (72.9%), reflecting ongoing graduate education. No college individuals show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (36.3%). (χ²=8561.286, df=24, Cramer's V=0.246, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association weakens to a weak effect (Cramer's V=0.111). The patterns observed at year 5 persist and clarify further. Less than associate degree (34.4%) and associate degree (33.1%) holders continue to show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment, while bachelor degree (31.3%) and master degree or higher (29.1%) holders show the highest rates of meaningful Minnesota employment. Master degree or higher holders show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (43.3%), suggesting the highest credential level is associated with the greatest geographic mobility and lowest regional retention. No college and some college individuals show relatively similar distributions across outcome categories, suggesting that without any credential attainment the long-term workforce trajectory is similar regardless of whether some postsecondary was attempted. (χ²=746.232, df=15, Cramer's V=0.111, p\<0.001) **Summary** Highest credential level shows a strong association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer's V=0.378) that weakens to a weak effect by year 10 (Cramer's V=0.111). The most substantively important finding is the clear and persistent inverse relationship between credential level and regional workforce attachment — sub-baccalaureate credential holders (less than associate and associate degree) show the strongest regional employment rates across all time points, while bachelor and master degree holders show increasing tendencies toward meaningful Minnesota employment and out-of-state migration. This pattern is consistent with and reinforces findings from the institution sector analysis, where public 2-year graduates showed the strongest regional attachment, and aligns with the broader pattern observed across academic achievement variables suggesting that higher educational attainment is associated with employment outside the region in Southwest Minnesota. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, highest.cred.level) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023") %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$highest.cred.level, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/Post-secondary/highest-cred-level-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

## `ps.grad.location` **Overview** Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between the location of postsecondary graduation (Did not graduate ps, PS grad MN, PS grad outside MN, PS grad region) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. This variable is uniquely relevant to the regional workforce development focus of this study, as it directly captures whether individuals pursued and completed postsecondary education within the Southwest Minnesota region, elsewhere in Minnesota, or outside the state. The association is weak but consistent across all three time points, with substantively compelling patterns in regional workforce attachment by graduation location. **Year 1** At one year post-graduation, graduation location shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer's V=0.158). Among those in the workforce rather than attending postsecondary, regional graduates show the strongest attachment to meaningful regional employment (56.2%), substantially higher than PS grad MN (35.5%), PS grad outside MN (38.2%), and did not graduate ps (24.6%). Did not graduate ps individuals show the highest rates of not meaningful employment (40.0%) and no Minnesota employment record (27.3%), while regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (6.2%), suggesting that graduating from a regional institution is strongly associated with immediate regional workforce engagement. (χ²=1514.441, df=9, Cramer's V=0.158, p\<0.001) **Year 5** By five years post-graduation the association strengthens modestly (Cramer's V=0.191). Regional graduates continue to show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (42.4%), considerably higher than PS grad MN (23.9%), PS grad outside MN (23.9%), and did not graduate ps (26.9%). PS grad MN graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (40.9%), while PS grad outside MN graduates show a strikingly high rate of no Minnesota employment record (47.4%), suggesting that graduating outside Minnesota is strongly associated with long-term out-of-state retention. Regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (13.4%), reinforcing the strong regional retention associated with regional graduation. (χ²=3181.250, df=9, Cramer's V=0.191, p\<0.001) **Year 10** At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer's V=0.162). Regional graduates continue to show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (36.9%), significantly higher than PS grad MN (20.4%), PS grad outside MN (18.0%), and did not graduate ps (24.8%). PS grad MN graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (38.0%), while PS grad outside MN graduates maintain the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (54.8%) — the highest rate of out-of-state retention observed for any subgroup across all variables examined. Regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (23.2%), the lowest of any graduation location group across all time points. (χ²=1582.788, df=9, Cramer's V=0.162, p\<0.001) **Summary** Postsecondary graduation location shows a weak but consistent and substantively compelling association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (Cramer's V=0.158, 0.191, 0.162). Despite the modest effect sizes, the findings tell a clear and policy-relevant story. Regional graduates show the strongest and most persistent attachment to meaningful regional employment at every time point, with rates consistently 10-15 percentage points higher than other graduation location groups by years 5 and 10. Conversely, graduating outside Minnesota is associated with the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record at all time points, reaching 54.8% by year 10. PS grad MN graduates occupy a middle position, showing strong meaningful Minnesota employment but moderate regional attachment. These findings strongly suggest that the location of postsecondary graduation is one of the most direct predictors of long-term regional workforce retention, with regional institutions playing a critical role in keeping graduates employed in Southwest Minnesota. ::: panel-tabset ### One year after graduating ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- meaningful.emp.sw %>% select(grad.year.1, ps.grad.location) %>% filter(grad.year.1 != "After 2023", grad.year.1 != "Attending ps", ps.grad.location != "Attending ps") %>% droplevels() tab_xtab(var.row = data$grad.year.1, var.col = data$ps.grad.location, title = "", show.exp = TRUE, show.col.prc = TRUE, file = "Data/Claude/analysis_local_employment_ct/Post-secondary/ps-grad-location-1.html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

# Overall Summary of Variable Associations with Workforce Participation Outcomes Cross-tabulation analysis with Cramer's V and one-way ANOVA with eta-squared were used to examine associations between independent variables and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation across four variable groups: demographics, high school characteristics, high school accomplishments, and postsecondary variables. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists reflecting their respective effect size measures. An important methodological note: several postsecondary variables show inflated Cramer's V values at year 1 due to structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category, and should be interpreted with this in mind. ## **Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer's V at Year 1** 1. PS Attendance (Cramer's V: 0.698, 0.295, 0.108) The strongest association at year 1 but substantially inflated by structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category. Association weakens considerably over time. Long-term finding: non-attendees show stronger regional attachment while attendees gravitate toward meaningful Minnesota employment. 2. PS Graduation (Cramer's V: 0.633, 0.330, 0.130) Similarly inflated at year 1 by structural overlap. Weakens considerably over time. Long-term finding: graduates show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment while non-graduates show stronger regional attachment and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record. 3. ACT Participation (Cramer's V: 0.430, 0.225, 0.137) The strongest non-structurally-inflated predictor and the most meaningful high school accomplishment variable. Non-ACT students show strong and persistent regional workforce attachment across all time points, while ACT takers are strongly associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent out-of-region employment. 4. Highest Credential Level (Cramer's V: 0.378, 0.246, 0.111) A strong association at year 1 that weakens over time. A clear inverse relationship emerges between credential level and regional attachment — sub-baccalaureate credential holders show the strongest regional employment rates while bachelor and master degree holders increasingly gravitate toward out-of-region employment and out-of-state migration. 5. PSEO Participation (Cramer's V: 0.370, 0.165, 0.087) Strong at year 1, largely reflecting direct relationship with postsecondary attendance. PSEO participants show persistent tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment over regional employment, suggesting broader geographic mobility associated with early college experience. 6. Economic Status (Cramer's V: 0.285, 0.127, 0.094) The strongest demographic predictor, particularly at year 1. Economically disadvantaged students enter the workforce earlier but into less stable employment, while non- disadvantaged students pursue postsecondary at higher rates. Differences narrow considerably by years 5 and 10. 7. Special Education Status (Cramer's V: 0.265, 0.149, 0.097) A moderate association at year 1 that weakens over time. Special education students enter the workforce earlier and show a persistent tendency toward regional over Minnesota employment across all time points. 8. AP Exam Participation (Cramer's V: 0.217, 0.146, 0.089) Moderate at year 1, weakening over time. Mirrors the ACT participation pattern — AP exam takers show persistent tendency toward out-of-region employment while non-takers show stronger regional attachment. 9. English Learner Status (Cramer's V: 0.214, 0.086, 0.059) Moderate at year 1, weakening considerably over time. English learners enter the workforce earlier but into less stable situations, with persistent challenges in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment through year 10. 10. Non-English Home Language (Cramer's V: 0.178, 0.058, 0.047) Closely mirrors English learner status throughout, consistent with the strong overlap between these variables identified during MCA. Slightly weaker associations at all time points. 11. PS Grad Location (Cramer's V: 0.158, 0.191, 0.162) A weak but remarkably stable association that is among the most substantively important findings of the entire analysis. Regional graduates show the strongest and most persistent regional employment attachment at every time point, while graduating outside Minnesota is associated with the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record, reaching 54.8% by year 10. 12. PS Grad Institution Sector (Cramer's V: 0.149, 0.161, 0.125) Weak but stable across all time points. Public 2-year institution graduates show the strongest regional attachment while private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest geographic mobility. Directly reinforces the graduation location findings. 13. Race/Ethnicity (Cramer's V: 0.108, 0.044, 0.047) Weak and declining association. Notable patterns include persistent workforce challenges for AI students and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record among all minority groups at year 10. Small sample sizes for minority groups warrant cautious interpretation. 14. Gender (Cramer's V: 0.097, 0.093, 0.056) Consistently weak across all time points. Females more likely to pursue postsecondary immediately after graduation while males transition more quickly into regional employment, though differences narrow considerably by year 10. 15. EDR (Cramer's V: 0.079, 0.110, 0.124) Weak but uniquely strengthening over time. EDR 6E Southwest Central students show a growing advantage in meaningful Minnesota employment while EDR 8 Southwest students show increasing rates of no Minnesota employment record, suggesting growing geographic divergence within the region. 16. CTE Achievement (Cramer's V: 0.075, 0.090, 0.088) The weakest categorical predictor but with a substantively important and stable pattern. CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment at every time point, with No CTE students showing strikingly high rates of no Minnesota employment record by year 10 (43.8%). 17. Community Demographic Description (Cramer's V: 0.057, 0.072, 0.079) The weakest categorical predictor overall but also strengthening over time. Urban/town/rural mix students increasingly gravitate toward out-of-region employment while town/rural mix and entirely rural students show stronger regional attachment. ## **Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared at Year 1** 1. MCA Math (η²: 0.168, 0.025, 0.017) The strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, the largest observed for any continuous variable. A distinctive early pattern shows lower Math scores associated with both not meaningful employment and no Minnesota employment record — unique among MCA subjects. By year 10 the meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest Math scores of all groups. 2. MCA Reading (η²: 0.129, 0.023, 0.057) The second strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, notable for its unique trajectory — weakening to a small effect at year 5 before strengthening to a medium effect at year 10. The only continuous variable to strengthen at year 10, suggesting Reading achievement becomes increasingly predictive of out-of-region employment over time. 3. ACT Composite Score (η²: 0.093, 0.038, 0.028) A moderate effect at year 1 weakening to small over time. The attending postsecondary group shows substantially higher scores than all workforce-engaged groups, and the meaningful regional employment group shows progressively lower scores relative to other groups over time. 4. MCA Science (η²: 0.085, 0.033, 0.019) A large effect at year 1 weakening to small over time. Results should be interpreted with caution given the voluntary and self-selected nature of Science MCA participation. Pattern mirrors Reading and Math, with regional employment consistently showing the lowest Science scores. 5. Total CTE Courses Taken (η²: 0.032, 0.027, 0.028) A small but remarkably stable effect across all three time points, unique among continuous variables. The meaningful regional employment group shows the highest number of CTE courses taken at every time point, with the gap between regional and out-of-region employment groups growing over time. 6. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²: 0.010, 0.004, 0.006) A negligible effect throughout, explaining at most 1% of variance. Despite very small effect sizes, regional employment consistently shows higher relative wages than meaningful Minnesota employment, suggesting competitive regional wages relative to the broader state labor market. 7. Average Unemployment Rate (η²: 0.005, 0.015, 0.032) The weakest predictor at year 1 but growing to a small effect by year 10. Individuals with no Minnesota employment record consistently experience lower unemployment rates, likely reflecting out-of-state migration to stronger labor markets. ## **Key Themes Across All Variable Groups** Three overarching themes emerge from the analysis: The first is a persistent academic achievement gradient in geographic mobility. Across virtually every academic achievement variable — ACT participation, AP exam, PSEO, MCA scores, ACT composite, and credential level — higher achievement is consistently associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent employment outside the region. This pattern strengthens over time and is one of the most robust findings of the entire analysis. The second is the importance of CTE and vocational pathways for regional retention. In direct contrast to the academic achievement pattern, CTE engagement variables — CTE achievement, total CTE courses taken, and by extension public 2-year institution graduation and sub-baccalaureate credentials — are consistently associated with stronger regional workforce attachment across all time points. This divergence between academic and CTE pathways has direct implications for regional workforce development policy. The third is the critical role of postsecondary geography. Where individuals attend and graduate from postsecondary education is among the most stable and policy-relevant predictors of long-term regional workforce retention. Regional postsecondary graduation is associated with the strongest regional employment attachment while out-of-state graduation is associated with the highest rates of permanent out-of-state migration. This finding points directly to the strategic importance of regional postsecondary institutions for Southwest Minnesota workforce development. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} master.after.ct <- meaningful.emp.sw write_csv(master.after.ct, "Data/SLEDS/Masters/After analysis/Master-after-ct.csv") ``` :::
